Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

The metric space $\mathbb C$ is complete. A sequence $z_n=x_n+iy_n$ converges to $x+iy$ exactly when $x_n\to x$ and $y_n\to y$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]], [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $\varphi(z, w, \bar p)$ be a formula of the language of set theory
([[def-language-of-set-theory]]) in which $A$ and $B$ do not occur free. The
**Replacement instance** for $\varphi$ is the sentence

$$\forall \bar p\,\forall A\,\Bigl(\forall z\,\bigl(z \in A \to \exists! w\,\varphi(z,w,\bar p)\bigr) \to \exists B\,\forall w\,\bigl(w \in B \leftrightarrow \exists z\,(z \in A \wedge \varphi(z,w,\bar p))\bigr)\Bigr).$$

The **Axiom Schema of Replacement** is the collection of all these sentences, one
for each such $\varphi$. In words: if for every $z \in A$ there is exactly one
$w$ with $\varphi(z,w,\bar p)$, then there is a set $B$ whose elements are
exactly those $w$.

derivations.claim: For each $i\in I$, the singleton finite-sum bound gives $|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|\le\|x^{(m)}-x^{(n)}\|_2$, so $(x_i^{(m)})_m$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb C$. By [F2] it has a unique limit $x_i$. These uniquely determined coordinates form a function $x:I\to\mathbb C$ by [A1]; no choices are made.

Let $x\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb C)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By [F1], $s=\|x\|_2^2$ is the supremum of its finite coordinate sums, so there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i|^2>s-\varepsilon^2$. For every finite $G\subseteq I\setminus F$, disjointness gives $\sum_{i\in G}|x_i|^2\le s-\sum_{i\in F}|x_i|^2<\varepsilon^2$. Thus the truncation $x|_F$ satisfies $\|x-x|_F\|_2<\varepsilon$, proving finite-support families are dense. The coordinate vectors have inner products $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$ by the canonical inner product in [F1], and their finite span is exactly the finitely supported families, so they form an orthonormal basis.

Since $(x^{(m)})$ is Cauchy, choose $N$ such that $\|x^{(m)}-x^{(n)}\|_2<1$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. Then $\|x^{(m)}\|_2\le\|x^{(N)}\|_2+1$ for $m\ge N$; the finitely many earlier norms have a finite maximum, so there is $M<\infty$ with $\|x^{(m)}\|_2\le M$ for every $m$. For any finite $F\subseteq I$, coordinate convergence and continuity of the finite sum give $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i|^2=\lim_m\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}|^2\le M^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ in [F1] shows $x\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb C)$.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so that $\|x^{(m)}-x^{(n)}\|_2<\varepsilon/2$ for all $m,n\ge N$. Fix $m\ge N$. For every finite $F\subseteq I$, coordinate convergence yields $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i|^2=\lim_n\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2\le\varepsilon^2/4$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ gives $\|x^{(m)}-x\|_2\le\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$. Hence $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I,\mathbb C)$ and every Cauchy sequence converges.
By [F1], $\ell^2(I,\mathbb C)$ is an inner-product space, and step 3.1 proves it is complete. It is therefore a Hilbert space by [F3]. The proof used no family of choices.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$. Let $F_n$ be the complex vector space with basis all finite words in the symbols $a_1,\ldots,a_n,a_1^\dagger,\ldots,a_n^\dagger$, including the empty word $1$. Give $F_n$ concatenation as multiplication and the conjugate-linear involution that reverses each word and exchanges $a_j$ with $a_j^\dagger$. Thus $F_n$ is the free unital complex $*$-algebra on $a_1,\ldots,a_n$.

For $x,y$ in an algebra write $\{x,y\}=xy+yx$. Let $J_n$ be the smallest two-sided $*$-ideal in $F_n$ containing

$$ \{a_i,a_j\},\qquad \{a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger\},\qquad \{a_i,a_j^\dagger\}-\delta_{ij}1\qquad(1\le i,j\le n). $$

Here a two-sided $*$-ideal is a complex linear subspace closed under left and right multiplication and under $*$. It exists as the intersection of all such ideals containing these relations; the collection is nonempty because it contains $F_n$. The relations are $*$-stable, since taking adjoints exchanges the first two families and changes the third relation with indices $i,j$ to the same relation with indices $j,i$. Define the **algebraic finite-mode CAR $*$-algebra** by $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n=F_n/J_n$, with generators denoted by the same symbols. Its quotient map gives the universal property: every tuple in a unital complex $*$-algebra satisfying these relations induces a unique unital $*$-homomorphism from $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n$. For $n=0$ there are no generators or relations and $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_0=\mathbb C$.

This definition is algebraic; the finite-mode universal C*-completion is identified in [[thm-finite-mode-car-algebra-is-full-matrix-algebra]].

derivations.claim: On basis vectors, $c_j^\dagger$ reverses exactly the same basis transition as $c_j$ and has the same real sign. Hence its matrix is the transpose-conjugate matrix of $c_j$. Each of $c_j^2$ and $(c_j^\dagger)^2$ vanishes because after one allowed toggle, the second toggle of the same type is forbidden. On a basis vector containing $j$, $c_j^\dagger c_j$ is the identity and $c_jc_j^\dagger$ is zero; when $j$ is absent these roles reverse. Thus $\{c_j,c_j^\dagger\}=I$.

Fix $j<k$. Whether the $j$-toggle is allowed depends only on membership of $j$, and whether the $k$-toggle is allowed depends only on membership of $k$. Therefore, if either toggle is forbidden, both orders of the two distinct toggles give zero. If both are allowed, performing the $j$-toggle first changes the number of occupied indices below $k$ by one, while the $k$-toggle does not change the number below $j$. The signs in the displayed formulas therefore differ by $-1$ when the order is reversed. This proves every distinct-mode anticommutator among $c_j,c_j^\dagger,c_k,c_k^\dagger$ is zero. Along with step 1.1 these are exactly [F1], so the specified map extends through the quotient to a $*$-representation $\pi_n$.

The operator $N_j$ is diagonal in the basis $e_S$, with eigenvalue $1$ when $j\in S$ and $0$ otherwise. Hence the commuting product $P_\varnothing$ is the projection onto $\mathbb C e_\varnothing$. For $T=\{j_1<\cdots<j_q\}$, the right-hand product $c_{j_q}\cdots c_{j_1}$ removes the elements of $T$ in increasing order; on $e_T$ each sign is $+1$, and on $e_U$ with $T\subsetneq U$ its result is a scalar multiple of $e_{U\setminus T}$. If $T\not\subseteq U$ it gives zero. The middle projection therefore kills every $e_U$ except $e_T$, and sends $e_T$ to $e_\varnothing$. The left-hand creation product sends $e_\varnothing$ to $e_S$, again with sign $+1$ because its indices are applied from largest to smallest. Thus $E_{S,T}e_U=\delta_{T,U}e_S$.

The operators $E_{S,T}$ are all standard matrix units relative to the basis $(e_S)_{S\in\mathcal P_n}$, so their linear span is $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)$. Each lies in the $*$-algebra generated by the $c_j,c_j^\dagger$, proving surjectivity. For $n=0$, the sole basis vector is $e_\varnothing$, $P_\varnothing=I$, and $E_{\varnothing,\varnothing}=I$, so the same conclusion holds.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. For each $k\ge0$, let $\Lambda^kH$ be the Hilbert exterior power with the Gram-determinant inner product and wedge convention of [[def-hilbert-exterior-power-and-induced-operator]], with $\Lambda^0H=\mathbb C$. The **fermionic Fock space** over $H$ is the Hilbert completion of the algebraic direct sum $\bigoplus_{k\ge0}^{\mathrm{alg}}\Lambda^kH$, where distinct particle-number summands are orthogonal and the inner product on a finite sum is the sum of the inner products of its components. The **vacuum vector** $\Omega$ is $1\in\Lambda^0H$.

On finite sums of decomposable wedges define the creation rule $C(f)\xi=f\wedge\xi$ for $f\in H$. This rule is initially defined on a dense subspace. Its bounded extension and the CAR relations for $C(f)$ and its Hilbert-space adjoint are proved in [[lem-fock-creation-annihilation-satisfy-car]].

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $n\ge0$. Set
$\Lambda^0H:=\mathbb C$. For $n\ge1$, the **algebraic $n$-fold tensor
product** $H^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}$ is the complex vector space generated by
symbols $x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n$ subject to complex linearity in each
slot. Equivalently, it is the quotient of the free complex vector space on
$H^n$ by the span of the coordinate-wise additivity and scalar-linearity
relations. Give it the sesquilinear form determined on elementary tensors by

$$\langle x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n, y_1\otimes\cdots\otimes y_n\rangle =\prod_{i=1}^n\langle x_i,y_i\rangle,$$

which is well defined because the product is linear in each first-slot vector
and conjugate-linear in each second-slot vector. Complete
$H^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}$ in the induced norm to obtain the Hilbert tensor
power $H^{\otimes n}$. Use the action convention
$U_\pi(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n)=
x_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{\pi^{-1}(n)}$ for $\pi\in S_n$.
The **Hilbert exterior power** $\Lambda^nH$ is the range of the orthogonal
projection

$$A_n:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi.$$

For $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in H$, write
$x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge x_n:=\sqrt{n!}\,A_n
(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n)$. Its inner product is

$$\langle x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge x_n, y_1\wedge\cdots\wedge y_n\rangle =\det[\langle x_i,y_j\rangle]_{i,j=1}^n.$$

If $T:H\to H$ is bounded, its **induced operator** $\Lambda^nT$ is the
restriction of $T^{\otimes n}$ to $\Lambda^nH$; equivalently
$(\Lambda^nT)(x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge x_n)=Tx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tx_n$.
Set $\Lambda^0T=I_{\mathbb C}$. For every bound $C$ of $T$, $C^n$ is a
bound for $\Lambda^nT$, and
$\Lambda^n(ST)=\Lambda^nS\,\Lambda^nT$ for bounded $S,T$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

For $x,y$ in an algebra write $\{x,y\}=xy+yx$. Let $J_n$ be the smallest two-sided $*$-ideal in $F_n$ containing

$$ \{a_i,a_j\},\qquad \{a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger\},\qquad \{a_i,a_j^\dagger\}-\delta_{ij}1\qquad(1\le i,j\le n). $$

It exists as the intersection of all such ideals containing these relations; the collection is nonempty because it contains $F_n$. The relations are $*$-stable, since taking adjoints exchanges the first two families and changes the third relation with indices $i,j$ to the same relation with indices $j,i$. Its quotient map gives the universal property: every tuple in a unital complex $*$-algebra satisfying these relations induces a unique unital $*$-homomorphism from $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n$. This definition is algebraic; the finite-mode universal C*-completion is identified in [[thm-finite-mode-car-algebra-is-full-matrix-algebra]].

A **possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra** is a complex vector space $A$
equipped with an associative complex-bilinear multiplication
$A \times A \to A$ ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]] for the bilinearity convention)
and a norm under which $A$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]],
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]), such that the norm is
**submultiplicative**:

$$\|ab\| \le \|a\|\,\|b\| \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

No multiplicative identity is assumed, and no real-algebra or unital
convention is imported from elsewhere.

A **complex C\*-algebra** is a possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra $A$
equipped with an **involution** $A \to A$, $a \mapsto a^*$, which is
conjugate-linear ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) and
satisfies

$$(a^*)^* = a, \qquad (ab)^* = b^*a^*, \qquad \|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2 \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

The last identity is the **C\*-identity**. Two immediate consequences are worth
recording, and both are proved from the displayed axioms alone:

- **the involution is isometric**: $\|a^*\| = \|a\|$. Indeed $\|a\|^2 = \|a^*a\| \le \|a^*\|\,\|a\|$ gives $\|a\| \le \|a^*\|$ when $a \ne 0$, and applying this inequality to $a^*$ and using $(a^*)^* = a$ gives $\|a^*\| \le \|a\|$; the case $a = 0$ is trivial;
- **no norm-uniqueness assertion is part of this definition**: such a theorem
  needs additional hypotheses and proof, and does not follow merely by naming
  the displayed C\*-identity.

bounded $*$-homomorphism, is a bounded complex-linear map
$\varphi : A \to B$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) satisfying

$$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b), \qquad \varphi(a^*) = \varphi(a)^* \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

A star-homomorphism is **not** required to be unital, and it is not required
that a unit be present or preserved; when $A$ and $B$ both happen to be unital,
$\varphi$ is called **unital** if $\varphi(1_A) = 1_B$. The bounded nonunital
star-homomorphisms are the arrows of the locally compact duality theorem on this
page ([[thm-locally-compact-gelfand-duality]]), with properness imposed there
through [[def-approximate-unit-and-proper-c-star-morphism]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. Order its finite-dimensional complex subspaces by inclusion. This is a directed system because the span $F+G$ of any two finite-dimensional subspaces is finite-dimensional. To each such $F$, assign the finite-dimensional CAR C*-algebra of [[thm-finite-dimensional-car-algebra-is-matrix-algebra]], with the generator-preserving maps of [[lem-car-finite-subspace-inclusions-are-isometric]]. Identify each stage with its image under these injective maps and let $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$ be their algebraic union.

The common finite-stage norm is well defined on this union because every inclusion is isometric. Define the **CAR C*-algebra over $H$**, $\mathsf{CAR}(H)$, to be the norm completion of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$. Addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and involution are the compatible finite-stage operations; their norm continuity makes them extend to the completion, and the C*-identity passes to limits. The identity is nonzero because the zero-dimensional stage is $\mathbb C$ and every inclusion preserves its unit. For $f\in H$, write $c(f)$ for the image of the generator in the stage $\operatorname{span}\{f\}$; the universal inductive-limit property and its norm are proved in [[thm-general-car-has-universal-inductive-limit-norm]].

If $F\subseteq G$ are finite-dimensional complex inner-product subspaces of a Hilbert space $H$, the generator-preserving map $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}(F)\to\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}(G)$ extends to an isometric unital $*$-homomorphism between their finite-dimensional C*-completions.

Let $F$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space of dimension $n$, and let $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}(F)$ be the algebra of [[def-finite-dimensional-car-algebra]]. For any orthonormal basis of $F$, the assignment to the $n$ standard finite-mode annihilation and creation generators identifies $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}(F)$ with $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n$. It therefore has a unique finite-dimensional universal C*-norm, and its completion is $*$-isomorphic to $M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$. Every unital $*$-representation of this completion on a nonzero Hilbert space is isometric.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. For each $k\ge0$, let $\Lambda^kH$ be the Hilbert exterior power with the Gram-determinant inner product and wedge convention of [[def-hilbert-exterior-power-and-induced-operator]], with $\Lambda^0H=\mathbb C$. The **fermionic Fock space** over $H$ is the Hilbert completion of the algebraic direct sum $\bigoplus_{k\ge0}^{\mathrm{alg}}\Lambda^kH$, where distinct particle-number summands are orthogonal and the inner product on a finite sum is the sum of the inner products of its components. The **vacuum vector** $\Omega$ is $1\in\Lambda^0H$.

On finite sums of decomposable wedges define the creation rule $C(f)\xi=f\wedge\xi$ for $f\in H$. This rule is initially defined on a dense subspace. Its bounded extension and the CAR relations for $C(f)$ and its Hilbert-space adjoint are proved in [[lem-fock-creation-annihilation-satisfy-car]].

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable, and let $\mathcal F_-(H)$ be its fermionic Fock space. The creation rule $C(f)\xi=f\wedge\xi$ extends to a bounded operator on $\mathcal F_-(H)$ with $\|C(f)\|=\|f\|$. Writing $A(f)=C(f)^*$ for its adjoint, one has, for all $f,g\in H$,

$$ \{C(f),C(g)\}=0,\qquad \{A(f),A(g)\}=0,\qquad \{A(f),C(g)\}=\langle g,f\rangle I. $$

Thus $f\mapsto C(f)$ is a bounded complex-linear CAR family in the convention of [[def-finite-dimensional-car-algebra]].

then $\mathcal B(X,Y)$ is Banach for the operator norm.

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. If
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ and $S \in \mathcal B(Y,Z)$, then

$$\|ST\| \le \|S\|\,\|T\|.$$

A **possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra** is a complex vector space $A$
equipped with an associative complex-bilinear multiplication
$A \times A \to A$ ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]] for the bilinearity convention)
and a norm under which $A$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]],
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]), such that the norm is
**submultiplicative**:

$$\|ab\| \le \|a\|\,\|b\| \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

No multiplicative identity is assumed, and no real-algebra or unital
convention is imported from elsewhere.

A **complex C\*-algebra** is a possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra $A$
equipped with an **involution** $A \to A$, $a \mapsto a^*$, which is
conjugate-linear ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) and
satisfies

$$(a^*)^* = a, \qquad (ab)^* = b^*a^*, \qquad \|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2 \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

The last identity is the **C\*-identity**. Two immediate consequences are worth
recording, and both are proved from the displayed axioms alone:

- **the involution is isometric**: $\|a^*\| = \|a\|$. Indeed $\|a\|^2 = \|a^*a\| \le \|a^*\|\,\|a\|$ gives $\|a\| \le \|a^*\|$ when $a \ne 0$, and applying this inequality to $a^*$ and using $(a^*)^* = a$ gives $\|a^*\| \le \|a\|$; the case $a = 0$ is trivial;
- **no norm-uniqueness assertion is part of this definition**: such a theorem
  needs additional hypotheses and proof, and does not follow merely by naming
  the displayed C\*-identity.

Let $A$ and $B$ be complex C\*-algebras. A **bounded star-homomorphism**, or
bounded $*$-homomorphism, is a bounded complex-linear map
$\varphi : A \to B$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) satisfying

$$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b), \qquad \varphi(a^*) = \varphi(a)^* \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

A star-homomorphism is **not** required to be unital, and it is not required
that a unit be present or preserved; when $A$ and $B$ both happen to be unital,
$\varphi$ is called **unital** if $\varphi(1_A) = 1_B$. The bounded nonunital
star-homomorphisms are the arrows of the locally compact duality theorem on this
page ([[thm-locally-compact-gelfand-duality]]), with properness imposed there
through [[def-approximate-unit-and-proper-c-star-morphism]].

citations.quote: For every integer $n\ge0$, the universal finite-mode CAR $*$-algebra $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n$ of [[def-finite-mode-car-algebra]] is $*$-isomorphic to $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)\cong M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$ under the occupation representation of [[lem-finite-mode-car-occupation-matrix-units]], where $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms under composition. Give this matrix algebra the operator norm and conjugate-transpose involution; it is a C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. Every unital $*$-representation on a nonzero Hilbert space is unitarily identified with the matrix action on the occupation coordinate tensored with the identity on one Hilbert space, and is therefore isometric. Consequently the universal C*-norm, the supremum of operator norms over these representations, equals the matrix norm, so the universal C*-completion is the same full matrix algebra.

Let $n\ge0$, let $V=\mathbb C^{2n}$ with ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_{2n}$, and put $Q(\sum_r z_re_r)=\sum_r z_r^2$. Use the plus-$Q$ convention of [[def-clifford-algebra-of-a-quadratic-space]]. Give $\mathrm{Cl}^+(V,Q)$ the conjugate-linear anti-involution that fixes each $e_r$; it is defined by conjugating coefficients, reversing words, and fixing the basis generators. Then there is a $*$-isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{Cl}^+(V,Q)\cong\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n $$

specified by

$$ e_{2j-1}\longmapsto \gamma_{2j-1}=a_j+a_j^\dagger,\qquad e_{2j}\longmapsto \gamma_{2j}=i(a_j^\dagger-a_j). $$

The inverse sends $a_j$ to $(e_{2j-1}+ie_{2j})/2$ and $a_j^\dagger$ to $(e_{2j-1}-ie_{2j})/2$. These are finite-mode algebra maps; they assert no relation between CAR and CCR.

derivations.claim: The displayed matrices act by $ae_\varnothing=0$, $ae_{\{1\}}=e_\varnothing$, $a^\dagger e_\varnothing=e_{\{1\}}$, and $a^\dagger e_{\{1\}}=0$. Thus $a^2=(a^\dagger)^2=0$, while $aa^\dagger=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $a^\dagger a=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, so $\{a,a^\dagger\}=I$. This verifies the one-mode CAR relations.

Substitution into the Majorana formulas gives the two displayed Pauli matrices. Direct multiplication gives $\gamma_1^2=\gamma_2^2=I$ and $\gamma_1\gamma_2+\gamma_2\gamma_1=0$; both matrices are self-adjoint. Hence they represent the two orthogonal plus-$Q$ Clifford generators.

The four matrices $aa^\dagger$, $a$, $a^\dagger$, and $a^\dagger a$ are respectively the matrix units $E_{00},E_{01},E_{10},E_{11}$, so the one-mode algebra is all of $M_2(\mathbb C)$, as asserted by the finite-mode theorem.

For $n\ge0$, let $\mathcal P_n$ be the set of subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $\mathcal F_n=\ell^2(\mathcal P_n)$ with orthonormal basis $e_S$ for $S\in\mathcal P_n$. For $1\le j\le n$ define operators on this finite-dimensional Hilbert space by

$$ c_j e_S=\begin{cases}0&j\notin S,\\(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s<j\}|}e_{S\setminus\{j\}}&j\in S,\end{cases}\qquad c_j^\dagger e_S=\begin{cases}(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s<j\}|}e_{S\cup\{j\}}&j\notin S,\\0&j\in S.\end{cases} $$

Then $c_j^\dagger$ is the Hilbert-space adjoint of $c_j$, and $a_j\mapsto c_j$, $a_j^\dagger\mapsto c_j^\dagger$ defines a $*$-representation $\pi_n:\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n\to\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)$. Put $N_j=c_j^\dagger c_j$ and $P_\varnothing=\prod_{j=1}^n(I-N_j)$, with the empty product equal to $I$. For $S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_p\}$ and $T=\{j_1<\cdots<j_q\}$, set

$$ E_{S,T}=c_{i_1}^\dagger\cdots c_{i_p}^\dagger P_\varnothing c_{j_q}\cdots c_{j_1}, $$

with empty operator products equal to $I$. Then $E_{S,T}e_U=\delta_{T,U}e_S$. Consequently the image of $\pi_n$ is all of $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)\cong M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$.

For every integer $n\ge0$, the universal finite-mode CAR $*$-algebra $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n$ of [[def-finite-mode-car-algebra]] is $*$-isomorphic to $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)\cong M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$ under the occupation representation of [[lem-finite-mode-car-occupation-matrix-units]], where $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms under composition. Give this matrix algebra the operator norm and conjugate-transpose involution; it is a C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. Every unital $*$-representation on a nonzero Hilbert space is unitarily identified with the matrix action on the occupation coordinate tensored with the identity on one Hilbert space, and is therefore isometric. Consequently the universal C*-norm, the supremum of operator norms over these representations, equals the matrix norm, so the universal C*-completion is the same full matrix algebra.

derivations.claim: Reading columns of the displayed matrices gives $a_1e_{\{1,2\}}=e_{\{2\}}$ and $a_2e_{\{1,2\}}=-e_{\{1\}}$. Applying the operators in the reverse order gives $a_2a_1e_{\{1,2\}}=e_\varnothing$ and $a_1a_2e_{\{1,2\}}=-e_\varnothing$, while both products vanish on the other three basis vectors. Hence $\{a_1,a_2\}=0$. The adjoint matrices give the corresponding creation relations, and their same-mode products satisfy $a_je_j=0$, $a_j^\dagger e_{S}=0$ when $j\in S$, and $\{a_j,a_j^\dagger\}=I$ on each of the four basis vectors.

For the mixed distinct-mode relation, on $e_{\{1\}}$ one has $a_1a_2^\dagger e_{\{1\}}=-e_{\{2\}}$ and $a_2^\dagger a_1e_{\{1\}}=e_{\{2\}}$; on $e_\varnothing,e_{\{2\}},e_{\{1,2\}}$ both terms sum to zero by the displayed matrices. Thus $\{a_1,a_2^\dagger\}=0$. This confirms the sign convention for modes in the order $1<2$.

By [F1], $P_\varnothing=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,0,0)$. The operator $a_1^\dagger P_\varnothing a_2$ sends $e_{\{2\}}$ to $e_{\{1\}}$ and kills the other three basis vectors, so it is the matrix unit $E_{\{1\},\{2\}}$. Together with the general formula in [F1], this is one explicit off-diagonal matrix unit inside the algebra $M_4(\mathbb C)$ of [F2].

citations.quote: Let $\pi_F$ be the countable-mode occupation representation on $\mathcal F_\infty$ and let $\alpha$ be the particle-hole automorphism of [[lem-countable-mode-car-particle-hole-automorphism]]. Then $\pi_F$ and $\pi_{\mathrm h}:=\pi_F\circ\alpha$ are irreducible representations of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathbb N}$, and they are not unitarily equivalent. Here two representations are unitarily equivalent if a unitary operator between their Hilbert spaces intertwines their actions. This proves existence of inequivalent irreducible representations; it does not classify all representations.

derivations.claim: The automorphism $\alpha(a_j)=a_j^\dagger$ is defined on the same countable-mode CAR algebra, so composing the Fock representation with $\alpha$ gives another representation of that algebra.
By [F1], this representation is irreducible but not unitarily equivalent to $\pi_F$. It is therefore a counterexample to the universal claim that every irreducible representation is Fock-equivalent.
